units.title: Unit 21 — Houses, flats and rooms
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 46–47 (PDF pages 50–51).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Topics: Leisure and lifestyle · accommodation and home
learningObjectives: Discuss accommodation types, rental advertisements, furnished properties and common pricing terms.
Describe the layout, condition and atmosphere of rooms and homes with natural adjective–noun combinations.
Distinguish move into from move out of and use accurate verbs for mortgages, extensions and refurbishing.
Use expressions with home to talk about independence, belonging, homecomings and holidays.

items.pt: acomodação para aluguel de curta duração
items.example: The visiting researcher found short-let accommodation near the campus.
items.note: Short-let describes accommodation rented for a limited period; it is common in British property advertisements.

items.example: We plan to move into a flat closer to the train station next month.
items.note: Move into refers to beginning to live in a property; contrast with move out of.

items.word: a wide range of suitable accommodation
items.pt: uma ampla variedade de opções de moradia adequadas
items.example: The housing office offers a wide range of suitable accommodation for new students.
items.note: A wide range of means many different options; accommodation is uncountable in this meaning.

items.example: They chose a fully furnished flat because they did not own any furniture.
items.note: Fully furnished means supplied with the main furniture needed to live there. Fully is an adverb modifying furnished.

items.example: Several small houses are available to rent in that neighbourhood.
items.note: Available to rent refers to a property being offered for rental, not necessarily for purchase.

items.pt: uma área residencial; um bairro residencial
items.example: The apartment is in a residential area away from noisy factories.
items.note: Residential describes an area mainly used for housing rather than business or industry.

items.example: The advertised rent is £900 per calendar month, excluding bills.
items.note: A common British rental-pricing expression; a calendar month is not automatically four weeks.

items.pt: um apartamento tipo estúdio; uma kitnet
items.example: A studio flat would be enough for someone living alone.
items.note: A studio flat normally combines living and sleeping space in one main room.

items.example: We viewed a newly built apartment with good insulation.
items.note: Newly built describes a property completed recently; compare an older property that has been refurbished.

items.example: The university offers spacious accommodation for families.
items.note: Spacious means having plenty of room; spatial is not the appropriate adjective here.

items.pt: uma cozinha totalmente equipada com instalações e armários
items.example: The holiday flat has a fully fitted kitchen with a cooker and cupboards.
items.note: A fitted kitchen has built-in units and equipment; this does not necessarily mean it contains every utensil.

items.pt: estacionamento fora da via pública; vaga interna
items.example: Off-road parking is useful when the street is busy.
items.note: Off-road parking refers to space away from the public roadway; parking, not park, names the facility.

items.example: An unfurnished flat is often cheaper, but you must supply your own furniture.
items.note: Unfurnished contrasts with furnished and fully furnished.

items.example: There is a flat to let above the bakery.
items.note: To let in British property notices means offered for rent, not for sale.

items.example: After years of saving, they found their dream home beside a lake.
items.note: Dream home is a home that closely matches what someone has always wanted.

items.example: The family restored a four-storey house in the old town.
items.note: Storey is British English for a level of a building; the plural is storeys.

items.example: Our new apartment has a spacious living room for family gatherings.
items.note: Spacious describes a room with plenty of space.

items.word: a wonderful view of the park
items.example: The top-floor room has a wonderful view of the park.
items.note: A view of names what can be seen from a place; compare overlook for a room facing something.

items.example: She works in a cosy study filled with books.
items.note: Cosy is British spelling and describes a small, warm and comfortable space.

items.example: The house has light and airy bedrooms with large windows.
items.note: Light and airy is a common positive description of bright, well-ventilated rooms.

items.example: The upstairs windows overlook the garden.
items.note: Here overlook means have a view over, not fail to notice something.

items.example: He rents a basement flat beneath the main house.
items.note: Basement describes the lower, partly or entirely below-ground level.

items.pt: uma edícula ou apartamento independente anexo para familiar
items.example: They built a granny flat so her father could live nearby.
items.note: A small, relatively independent dwelling attached to or near a larger house; it is not limited to grandmothers.

items.word: turn a garage into a granny flat
items.pt: transformar uma garagem em moradia anexa
items.example: They hope to turn a garage into a granny flat for a relative.
items.note: Turn A into B expresses changing the use or function of a space.

items.example: They want to add an extension to make space for a home office.
items.note: An extension is extra building space added to an existing property.

items.example: We may build an extension behind the kitchen.
items.note: Build an extension is another natural verb partnership with extension.

items.example: The old flat was completely refurbished before the new tenants arrived.
items.note: Refurbish means renovate or improve an existing property, not necessarily construct a new one.

items.example: They spent two summers doing up an old house in the countryside.
items.note: Do up is a fairly informal British phrasal verb for repairing and redecorating.

items.pt: sair de um apartamento; mudar-se de um apartamento
items.example: I must move out of a flat at the end of my lease.
items.note: Move out of is the opposite of move into; do not use move off in this housing sense.

items.example: He stayed in a one-room flat during his first year in London.
items.note: One-room describes a flat with only one main room; it does not necessarily mean there is no bathroom.

items.pt: um prédio deteriorado; uma construção em ruínas
items.example: The council plans to restore a dilapidated building near the station.
items.note: Dilapidated means in poor condition after long neglect.

items.pt: um hall com correntes de ar
items.example: A draughty hall made the entrance feel cold in winter.
items.note: Draughty means letting unpleasant currents of air through; it does not mean windy outdoors.

items.example: We walked through a chilly corridor to reach the classroom.
items.note: Chilly means unpleasantly or noticeably cold, often indoors.

items.example: The small desk barely fitted into the cramped room.
items.note: Cramped describes a space too small for comfortable movement.

items.pt: um lugar só meu; minha própria moradia
items.example: After sharing houses for years, I finally have a place of my own.
items.note: A place of my own means a home for my use, whether owned or rented; a place of your own changes with the speaker.

items.example: The city needs more affordable housing for young workers.
items.note: Affordable means within people’s financial reach; buyable is not the usual adjective.

items.example: A shortage of affordable housing has forced some residents to move away.
items.note: A shortage of indicates that there is not enough of something.

items.example: They decided to take out a mortgage rather than spend all their savings.
items.note: Take out a mortgage means arrange a housing loan; get out a mortgage is incorrect.

items.pt: uma festa de inauguração da casa nova; um chá de casa nova
items.example: We held a house-warming party after we finished unpacking.
items.note: A house-warming party celebrates moving into a new home.

items.pt: sair da casa da família para morar em outro lugar
items.example: Many students leave home when they start university.
items.note: Leave home often means begin living independently rather than simply go outside.

items.example: It can be difficult to move away from your family for a new job.
items.note: Move away from emphasises geographical separation, unlike move out, which focuses on leaving a home.

items.pt: sentir saudade de casa; sentir falta da família e do lar
items.example: She began to feel homesick during her first month abroad.
items.note: Homesick describes missing your home or familiar surroundings.

items.pt: dar uma festa; organizar uma festa
items.example: Our neighbours plan to throw a party to celebrate the new house.
items.note: Throw a party is an informal, common alternative to organise or hold a party.

items.example: Her friends gathered at the airport to welcome her home.
items.note: Welcome someone home describes greeting a person on their return home.

items.pt: fique à vontade; sinta-se em casa
items.example: Please make yourself at home while I prepare some tea.
items.note: A friendly invitation to relax and feel comfortable in someone else’s home.

items.pt: sentir-se em casa; sentir-se à vontade
items.example: He quickly began to feel at home in his new neighbourhood.
items.note: Feel at home means feel relaxed, welcome or familiar in a place.

items.pt: uma segunda residência; casa de férias
items.example: They bought a second home by the coast for weekends.
items.note: A second home is an additional residence, often used for holidays.

units.title: Unit 22 — Eating and drinking
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 48–49 (PDF pages 52–53).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Topics: Leisure and lifestyle · food and eating
learningObjectives: Distinguish common categories of food, including fresh produce, ready meals, additives and perishable products.
Describe meal size and quality using light, substantial, hearty, slap-up and gourmet accurately.
Use natural expressions for appetite, snacks, restaurant menus and price.
Distinguish an individual national meal from a country’s food or cuisine and recognise typical learner errors.

items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: The children tend to choose junk food when they visit the cinema.
items.note: Junk food refers to food with little nutritional value, often high in salt, sugar or fat.

items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: The café offers nourishing meals made with vegetables and beans.
items.note: Nourishing describes food that supports health and provides useful nutrients.

items.pt: produtos agrícolas frescos; frutas e hortaliças frescas
items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: The local market sells fresh produce every morning.
items.note: Produce is a noun for farm products, especially fruit and vegetables; in this sense it is pronounced /ˈprɒdjuːs/.

items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: The shop has a separate shelf for organic food.
items.note: Organic refers to food produced according to specific farming standards; it does not literally mean no chemicals are present.

items.pt: refeições prontas para aquecer ou consumir
items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: Ready meals are useful when I get home too late to cook.
items.note: A ready meal is prepared in advance and usually needs only heating.

items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: The label lists the food additives used in the sauce.
items.note: Additives are substances added for purposes such as flavour, texture, appearance or preservation.

items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: Regular exercise can benefit your long-term health.
items.note: Long-term describes effects or outcomes over an extended period; it does not mean immediately.

items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: Some processed foods contain a lot of added salt.
items.note: Processed describes foods altered from their original state; the degree of processing can vary.

items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: The report compares labelling rules for GM foods in several countries.
items.note: GM stands for genetically modified; the term describes a production method, not a single nutritional property.

items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: Keep perishable food cold during the journey.
items.note: Perishable food can spoil relatively quickly if it is not stored correctly.

items.section: A · Talking about types of food
items.example: Several guests reported food poisoning after the event.
items.note: Food poisoning refers to illness caused by contaminated food; get food poisoning is a common verb combination.

items.example: I had a light meal before the evening lecture.
items.note: Light describes a meal that is not particularly large or heavy.

items.pt: uma refeição farta; uma refeição reforçada
items.example: After the hike, we needed a substantial meal.
items.note: Substantial suggests a filling or fairly large meal.

items.pt: um banquete; uma refeição caprichada e farta
items.example: They treated the whole team to a slap-up meal after the competition.
items.note: An informal British expression for an unusually good and often large meal.

items.example: We booked a small restaurant for a gourmet meal on our anniversary.
items.note: Gourmet suggests especially refined or high-quality cooking rather than simply a large portion.

items.example: After a week of travelling, she missed home-cooked food.
items.note: Home-cooked food is prepared in a home-style way rather than sold as a ready meal.

items.example: I usually have a quick snack between meetings.
items.note: Have is a common verb for eating or drinking; a snack is smaller than a full meal.

items.example: A cold glass of water was a refreshing drink after the run.
items.note: Refreshing means helping someone feel cooler, more awake or less thirsty.

items.pt: morrendo de fome; com muita fome
items.example: By the time we reached the hotel, we were dying of hunger.
items.note: A conversational exaggeration meaning extremely hungry, not necessarily literally starving.

items.example: There is time to eat a decent meal before the concert.
items.note: Decent often means satisfactory and substantial enough for the situation, not necessarily expensive.

items.example: My younger brother has a healthy appetite after football practice.
items.note: A healthy appetite means a normal or good desire for food, usually positively viewed.

items.example: We had a hearty breakfast before the long drive.
items.note: Hearty describes a substantial and satisfying meal, often served in the morning.

items.pt: um refrigerante ou outra bebida não alcoólica
items.example: She ordered a soft drink while her friends chose coffee.
items.note: Soft drink usually means a non-alcoholic drink, especially a bottled fizzy drink; it does not mean a warm drink.

items.pt: um almoço de verdade; um almoço completo
items.example: Take a break and have a proper lunch instead of eating at your desk.
items.note: Proper emphasises a satisfactory, complete meal rather than a small snack.

items.pt: tirar seu apetite; estragar a fome para a refeição
items.example: Too many biscuits now will spoil your appetite for dinner.
items.note: Spoil your appetite means reduce your wish to eat at the next meal.

items.pt: um menu fechado; um cardápio de preço fixo
items.example: The bistro offers a set menu with a starter and a main course.
items.note: A set menu offers a limited selection of courses for a fixed price.

items.pt: com preço razoável; com preço justo
items.example: We found a reasonably priced café near the museum.
items.note: Reasonably priced means not too expensive for what is offered.

items.example: The restaurant has a pleasant setting beside the river.
items.note: Setting describes the surroundings or atmosphere in which a meal is enjoyed.

items.section: C · Common mistakes and food terminology
items.example: The hotel restaurant specialises in international cuisine.
items.note: Cuisine refers to a style or tradition of cooking; worldwide cuisine is not the usual expression.

items.section: C · Common mistakes and food terminology
items.example: The festival included stalls serving international food.
items.note: International food refers to dishes from different countries; international is the natural adjective here.

items.pt: uma refeição francesa; uma refeição típica francesa
items.section: C · Common mistakes and food terminology
items.example: They prepared a French meal for the visiting students.
items.note: Use a French meal for an individual dining occasion; French cuisine refers to the broader cooking tradition.

items.section: C · Common mistakes and food terminology
items.example: Her cookbook introduces readers to French cuisine.
items.note: Cuisine is a general style of cooking; it does not describe one particular meal.

items.example: Despite a large dinner, he still had an insatiable appetite.
items.note: Insatiable means impossible to satisfy; it is stronger than a healthy appetite.

items.example: At the training centre, athletes receive three decent meals a day.
items.note: The exercise contrasts full, satisfying meals with a lighter eating pattern.

items.example: They invited us over for a home-cooked meal.
items.note: A home-cooked meal is prepared at home; compare home-cooked food as a general category.

items.example: You can get food poisoning from food that has not been stored safely.
items.note: Get food poisoning is a natural way to describe becoming ill from contaminated food.

items.word: take a friend out to dinner
items.pt: levar um amigo para jantar fora; pagar um jantar a um amigo
items.example: I want to take a friend out to dinner to celebrate her new job.
items.note: Take someone out to dinner means invite them to eat away from home, often as a treat.
